options: The straight-line change from its initial position to its final position
The total length of the path traveled
The average of all the distances along a trip
questions.explanation: Displacement is the net change in position — one straight vector from the initial spot to the final spot.
questions.misconception: Learners often equate displacement with total path length; the path is distance, displacement ignores it.

questions.prompt: A student walks 6 m forward then 4 m back from the start. What is the displacement?
questions.explanation: Net change: 6 m forward, minus the 4 m returned = 2 m still forward. Direction matters because displacement is a vector.
questions.misconception: A common error is averaging the two legs (5 or 4 m) instead of subtracting — displacement is a net difference, not an average.

questions.prompt: A runner goes around a 200 m circular track and returns exactly to the starting line. What is the displacement at the finish?
questions.explanation: Since the start and final position are the same point, displacement is zero regardless of the 200 m of distance traveled.
questions.misconception: Students pick the track length 200 m — that's distance. Displacement asks 'where did I end compared with where I started' and the answer is nowhere new.

questions.prompt: Two legs: 3 m east then 4 m east. What is the net displacement?
questions.explanation: Same direction legs add together: 3 + 4 = 7 m east. Tip-to-tail keeps them pointing the same way.
questions.misconception: Some reverse one arrow mentally and get 1 m; reversed signs cancel only when directions oppose each other.

questions.prompt: Velocity uses displacement instead of distance. What is the main reason?
options: Velocity is a vector and needs a direction, just like displacement
Distance is never measured in meters
Displacement is always a bigger number
questions.explanation: Velocity is displacement per unit time, so it inherits the direction of the displacement — that's why velocity, not speed, is a vector.
questions.misconception: Factoids about speed being directionless get inverted here: speed is the scalar that uses distance; velocity is the vector that uses displacement.
